claims.text: The nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a disordered solid-solution structure.
A disordered solid solution is typical of high-entropy alloys.
In situ HRTEM equipped with a controlled heating holder can directly observe atomic-scale structural evolution during heating.
Such observations can provide experimental evidence for testing theoretical predictions of enhanced thermal stability.
Controlled incremental heating during HRTEM is the proposed intervention.
An inert or vacuum TEM environment will prevent extraneous oxidation or environmental effects from obscuring thermally induced changes.
Heating may modify atomic arrangements in the nanoparticles.
Thermodynamic contributions may promote diffusion-restricted stabilization in heated AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Thermodynamic contributions may instead induce transient atomic rearrangements during heating.
HRTEM can capture the proposed heating-induced atomic dynamics in real time.
Minimal atomic reorganization during heating would indicate enhanced thermal stability.
A maintained or slowly evolving atomic structure up to a critical temperature would support enhanced thermal stability.
Abrupt atomic rearrangement or decomposition during heating would challenge the enhanced-stability prediction.
Electron-beam interactions may influence the observed structural dynamics.
Diffraction-pattern changes can indicate phase or structural transitions.
A lack of thermally induced atomic-scale structural changes would falsify the proposed validation of thermal-stability predictions.

contradictions.description: The mechanism and predicted outcome treat minimal or absent atomic reorganization as evidence of enhanced stability, whereas the falsification rule says that observing no thermally induced structural changes would falsify the hypothesis.
